headline: Case made for as a high-quality fund manager trading at an attractive valuation despite office sector headwinds and interest rate pressures
reasoning: Charter Hall has delivered ~11.5% p.a. total return since its 2006 IPO, driven by its transition from a traditional REIT to a fund manager that generates fees on client capital with minimal incremental investment required. Around two-thirds of its FUM is in non-office sectors such as Industrial & Logistics, Equities, Retail, and Social Infrastructure, making the 'office is dead' critique partially unfair. CHC's office portfolio skews to newer, better-located buildings with 96% occupancy versus an 85% national average and a high-quality tenant base. Interest rate headwinds have frozen transaction activity and weighed on valuations, but with rates at 10-year highs and inflation falling, Airlie argues rates have likely peaked, which should restore transaction activity and offset FUM devaluations. At ~15x FY24 EPS guidance, Airlie believes current pricing more than captures the risks and represents an opportunity to own a high-quality business at an attractive valuation.
quote: We believe these risks are more than captured in CHC's current price and have provided the opportunity to invest in a high-quality business at an attractive valuation. We don't disagree that the 'Work From Home' trend has created meaningful challenges for the Office sector. Corporates have quite reasonably concluded they can achieve substantial rent savings while providing their workforce with increased flexibility. This has resulted in an increase in market vacancy and placed pressure on rents. This has understandably weighed on Charter Hall, with the share price down 48% since its peak of $21.83 in 2021. While Charter Hall will undoubtedly be affected by weakness in Office, we believe the criticism is not entirely fair given roughly two-thirds of its Funds Under Management (FUM) is in 'non-office' sectors, including Industrial and Logistics (28%), Equities (18%), Retail (16%) and Social Infrastructure (4%).

headline: Airlie highlights Charter Hall as an undervalued quality business within the REIT sector, with FUM growing at 17% CAGR over the decade and a 19% p.a. total shareholder return since listing.
reasoning: Charter Hall has delivered a total shareholder return of 19% per annum since listing in 2005, driven by its transition from a traditional REIT to one of Australia's largest property funds management businesses. FUM has grown at a 17% CAGR to over $52bn, with the funds management business reaching an inflection point that should continue to drive strong outcomes. Key quality attributes include sticky wholesale capital (~7 years between redemption windows), 77% of revenue from recurring annuity-style fees, high-quality tenants including government (12.5%) and major retailers, and the scale advantage of being able to compete for assets over $1bn and complete a high proportion of transactions off-market. Airlie sees a step change in business quality driven by increasing scale and lower capital requirements, which should continue to drive outstanding financial results for shareholders.
quote: There's a lot to like about Charter Hall's funds management business: The funds own a selection of high-quality assets with some of Australia's most sought-after tenants (Government account for 12.5% of rental income, Woolworths 6.4%, Wesfarmers 5.9%, and Coles 5.2%). Wholesale capital is relatively 'sticky' with ~7yrs between redemption windows. This means investors can't simply pull their money out at once, enhancing the stability of earnings. High contribution from recurring, annuity-style funds management fees and property services revenue (77% of CY20 funds management revenue). Scale begets scale – Charter Hall are one of only a handful of managers that can compete for assets >$1bn in value. A high proportion of transactions for Charter Hall are completed off-market, meaning less competition for those assets.
